name: Padimate A

lead: Padimate A is a PABA-derived UV filter, a close relative of padimate O. It saw limited use in sunscreens but is not a current mainstream ingredient.
Very little padimate A-specific research is available.

paras: Like other PABA esters it absorbs UVB through its aminobenzoate structure.
Wikipedia reports it was withdrawn in Europe in 1989 and never approved in the US, and that padimates raised photochemical safety questions in cell studies. No clinical studies were found.

lead: Padimate A (isoamyl p-dimethylaminobenzoate, Escalol 506) is a PABA-ester UV filter, a dimethylated ester of 4-aminobenzoic acid.[1] It is chemically related to padimate O (octyl dimethyl PABA), a much more widely studied sunscreen ingredient.[1] Wikipedia states it was withdrawn in Europe in 1989 and was never approved for use in sunscreens in the US.[1]

Published concerns about the padimate class involve photochemistry: Wikipedia reports that padimate A and padimate O resemble an industrial free-radical generator and increased the lethal effects of UV on cells in cited studies.[1] Little padimate A-specific research was found, and no clinical studies exist in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Withdrawn in Europe 1989; not approved in the US for sunscreens (per Wikipedia)[1]

paras: Padimate A has a melting point below 25 degrees C and is the isoamyl analogue of the better-known padimate O.[1]

Wikipedia notes that the compound was withdrawn in Europe in 1989 for unstated reasons and was never approved for US sunscreens.[1] It also reports that the photochemistry of padimates, including increased UV lethality in cells, has been part of the sunscreen safety controversy.[1]

Related research on padimate O and other organic UV filters includes studies of skin penetration and keratinocyte toxicity of common sunscreens,[2] UV-induced suppression of contact hypersensitivity in relation to padimate O and oxybenzone,[3] and environmental occurrence of UV filters in wastewater and biota.[4][5] These do not isolate padimate A.

No studies found of padimate A. Registered sunscreen trials in the sources reviewed (for example, a phase 1 study of a padimate O nanoparticle sunblock in 13 people, and SPF testing of commercial products) concern padimate O or unspecified products.[6][7]

timeline.event: Padimate A reported withdrawn in Europe.[1]
